quests.question: During the lecture, try to listen ___ the professor instead of checking your phone.
quests.targetSentence: During the lecture, try to listen to the professor instead of checking your phone.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Listen to' is the fixed combination for paying attention to someone speaking; 'listen for' would mean waiting to detect a specific sound instead.
quests.nativeTip: This verb needs a word that connects it to the person being heard.
quests.visualAnchor: 🧭 Preposition 'to' (Direction & Spatial Relationship) ➔ 'During the lecture, try to listen to the professor instead of checking your phone.'

quests.question: Please wait ___ the receptionist to call your name.
quests.targetSentence: Please wait for the receptionist to call your name.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Wait for' is the standard combination when you're expecting something or someone to happen.
quests.nativeTip: You're waiting on behalf of an event that hasn't happened yet.
quests.visualAnchor: 🧭 Preposition 'for' (Direction & Spatial Relationship) ➔ 'Please wait for the receptionist to call your name.'

quests.question: Look ___ this photo — you can really see how much the city has changed.
quests.targetSentence: Look at this photo — you can really see how much the city has changed.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Look at' fits when directing attention toward something visible, like a photo.
quests.nativeTip: Your eyes are directed toward a specific object.
quests.visualAnchor: 🧭 Preposition 'at' (Specific Point (e.g. at the door)) ➔ 'Look at this photo — you can really see how much the city has changed.'

quests.question: This umbrella doesn't belong ___ me — I think it's yours.
quests.targetSentence: This umbrella doesn't belong to me — I think it's yours.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Belong to' is the fixed combination for showing that something is someone's property.
quests.nativeTip: This verb shows ownership, connecting an object to its owner.
quests.visualAnchor: 🧭 Preposition 'to' (Direction & Spatial Relationship) ➔ 'This umbrella doesn't belong to me — I think it's yours.'

quests.question: Whether we go hiking or not depends ___ the weather forecast.
quests.targetSentence: Whether we go hiking or not depends on the weather forecast.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Depend on' is the standard combination; 'depend of' is a common mistake carried over from other languages.
quests.nativeTip: One outcome relies on another condition being met.
quests.visualAnchor: 🧭 Preposition 'on' (Surface Contact (e.g. on the table)) ➔ 'Whether we go hiking or not depends on the weather forecast.'

quests.question: I already paid ___ the tickets online, so we can go straight in.
quests.targetSentence: I already paid for the tickets online, so we can go straight in.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Pay for' is used when naming the thing being purchased; 'pay to' doesn't fit this pattern.
quests.nativeTip: Money was exchanged in return for something.
quests.visualAnchor: 🧭 Preposition 'for' (Direction & Spatial Relationship) ➔ 'I already paid for the tickets online, so we can go straight in.'

quests.question: I need to talk ___ my manager about the schedule change.
quests.targetSentence: I need to talk to my manager about the schedule change.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Talk to' names the person you're speaking with, while 'talk about' would introduce the topic instead.
quests.nativeTip: This word connects the verb to the person being spoken with.
quests.visualAnchor: 🧭 Preposition 'to' (Direction & Spatial Relationship) ➔ 'I need to talk to my manager about the schedule change.'

quests.question: We talked ___ our vacation plans over dinner.
quests.targetSentence: We talked about our vacation plans over dinner.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Talk about' introduces the subject being discussed, unlike 'talk to', which names the person.
quests.nativeTip: This word introduces the topic of the conversation, not the listener.
quests.visualAnchor: 🧭 Preposition 'about' (Direction & Spatial Relationship) ➔ 'We talked about our vacation plans over dinner.'

quests.question: I don't agree ___ the new office policy — it feels unfair to remote workers.
quests.targetSentence: I don't agree with the new office policy — it feels unfair to remote workers.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Agree with' expresses sharing (or not sharing) an opinion about something already proposed; 'agree on' would fit reaching a new decision together, like agreeing on a price.
quests.nativeTip: This word connects the verb to the idea or person you share (or don't share) an opinion with.
quests.visualAnchor: 🧭 Preposition 'with' (Direction & Spatial Relationship) ➔ 'I don't agree with the new office policy — it feels unfair to remote workers.'

quests.question: She really cares ___ her students' wellbeing, always asking how they're coping outside class.
quests.targetSentence: She really cares about her students' wellbeing, always asking how they're coping outside class.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Care about' expresses concern for something abstract, like wellbeing; 'care for' usually pairs with directly looking after a person, pet, or plant.
quests.nativeTip: This describes emotional concern for an idea, not a hands-on duty like feeding or tending someone.
quests.visualAnchor: 🧭 Preposition 'about' (Direction & Spatial Relationship) ➔ 'She really cares about her students' wellbeing, always asking how they're coping outside class.'

quests.question: She applied ___ a scholarship to help cover her tuition.
quests.targetSentence: She applied for a scholarship to help cover her tuition.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Apply for' is used when naming the opportunity itself, such as a scholarship or a job; 'apply to' is reserved for naming an institution, like a university.
quests.nativeTip: The thing she's applying for is an opportunity, not an institution.
quests.visualAnchor: 🧭 Preposition 'for' (Direction & Spatial Relationship) ➔ 'She applied for a scholarship to help cover her tuition.'

quests.question: We arrived ___ the airport two hours before our flight.
quests.targetSentence: We arrived at the airport two hours before our flight.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Arrive at' fits specific points like an airport, a station, or a building.
quests.nativeTip: An airport is treated as a specific point, not a wide area.
quests.visualAnchor: 🧭 Preposition 'at' (Specific Point (e.g. at the door)) ➔ 'We arrived at the airport two hours before our flight.'

quests.conceptTitle: Preposition Radar: Contrast: arrive at vs arrive in
quests.spatialHierarchy: Enclosed Space / Volume (e.g. in the room)
quests.question: They arrived ___ Japan after a fourteen-hour flight.
quests.targetSentence: They arrived in Japan after a fourteen-hour flight.
quests.grammarRule: Contrast: arrive at vs arrive in
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Arrive in' is used for large areas like countries and cities, unlike 'arrive at', which suits a specific point.
quests.nativeTip: A whole country is a large area, not a single point.
quests.visualAnchor: 🧭 Preposition 'in' (Enclosed Space / Volume (e.g. in the room)) ➔ 'They arrived in Japan after a fourteen-hour flight.'

quests.conceptTitle: Preposition Radar: Contrast: arrive at vs arrive in
quests.question: The delivery driver should arrive ___ your doorstep within the hour.
quests.targetSentence: The delivery driver should arrive at your doorstep within the hour.
quests.grammarRule: Contrast: arrive at vs arrive in
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Arrive at' fits a specific point like a doorstep, following the same rule taught with the airport example.
quests.nativeTip: A doorstep is one exact spot, not a broad area.
quests.visualAnchor: 🧭 Preposition 'at' (Specific Point (e.g. at the door)) ➔ 'The delivery driver should arrive at your doorstep within the hour.'

quests.conceptTitle: Preposition Radar: Contrast: arrive at vs arrive in
quests.spatialHierarchy: Enclosed Space / Volume (e.g. in the room)
quests.question: We're flying to Rome tomorrow and should arrive ___ the city by early afternoon.
quests.targetSentence: We're flying to Rome tomorrow and should arrive in the city by early afternoon.
quests.grammarRule: Contrast: arrive at vs arrive in
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Arrive in' is correct because a city is a broad area, the same category as the country example earlier in this level.
quests.nativeTip: A city, like a country, counts as a large area.
quests.visualAnchor: 🧭 Preposition 'in' (Enclosed Space / Volume (e.g. in the room)) ➔ 'We're flying to Rome tomorrow and should arrive in the city by early afternoon.'

quests.question: My younger brother has always been good ___ solving puzzles.
quests.targetSentence: My younger brother has always been good at solving puzzles.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Good at' is the fixed combination for describing skill in a particular activity.
quests.nativeTip: This word connects a skill or ability to a specific activity.
quests.visualAnchor: 🧭 Preposition 'at' (Specific Point (e.g. at the door)) ➔ 'My younger brother has always been good at solving puzzles.'

quests.spatialHierarchy: Enclosed Space / Volume (e.g. in the room)
quests.question: She's always been interested ___ marine biology, ever since she was a kid.
quests.targetSentence: She's always been interested in marine biology, ever since she was a kid.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Interested in' is the standard combination for describing curiosity or enthusiasm toward a subject.
quests.nativeTip: This word links a feeling of curiosity to its subject.
quests.visualAnchor: 🧭 Preposition 'in' (Enclosed Space / Volume (e.g. in the room)) ➔ 'She's always been interested in marine biology, ever since she was a kid.'

quests.question: Many people are afraid ___ public speaking, even experienced professionals.
quests.targetSentence: Many people are afraid of public speaking, even experienced professionals.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Afraid of' expresses fear toward the thing named; 'afraid for' would instead mean feeling worried about someone else's safety.
quests.nativeTip: This describes fear of an activity itself, not worry on someone else's behalf.
quests.visualAnchor: 🧭 Preposition 'of' (Direction & Spatial Relationship) ➔ 'Many people are afraid of public speaking, even experienced professionals.'

quests.question: Her parents are incredibly proud ___ her decision to study abroad.
quests.targetSentence: Her parents are incredibly proud of her decision to study abroad.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Proud of' is the fixed combination for expressing pride about an achievement or decision.
quests.nativeTip: This word links pride to its cause.
quests.visualAnchor: 🧭 Preposition 'of' (Direction & Spatial Relationship) ➔ 'Her parents are incredibly proud of her decision to study abroad.'

quests.question: This small town is famous ___ its handmade cheese.
quests.targetSentence: This small town is famous for its handmade cheese.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Famous for' names the reason something is well known; 'famous of' is a common but incorrect substitution.
quests.nativeTip: This word connects a reputation to the reason behind it.
quests.visualAnchor: 🧭 Preposition 'for' (Direction & Spatial Relationship) ➔ 'This small town is famous for its handmade cheese.'

quests.question: As team leader, she's responsible ___ making sure deadlines are met.
quests.targetSentence: As team leader, she's responsible for making sure deadlines are met.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Responsible for' names a task or duty; 'responsible to' would instead name the person or group someone answers to, like a board.
quests.nativeTip: This links a duty to the task itself, not to a person in authority.
quests.visualAnchor: 🧭 Preposition 'for' (Direction & Spatial Relationship) ➔ 'As team leader, she's responsible for making sure deadlines are met.'

quests.question: This recipe is similar ___ the one my grandmother used to make.
quests.targetSentence: This recipe is similar to the one my grandmother used to make.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Similar to' is the fixed combination for comparing two things that resemble each other.
quests.nativeTip: This word links two things being compared as alike.
quests.visualAnchor: 🧭 Preposition 'to' (Direction & Spatial Relationship) ➔ 'This recipe is similar to the one my grandmother used to make.'

quests.question: My approach to teaching is quite different ___ my colleague's.
quests.targetSentence: My approach to teaching is quite different from my colleague's.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Different from' is the most widely accepted form for contrasting two things across formal English.
quests.nativeTip: This links two things being compared as unlike each other.
quests.visualAnchor: 🧭 Preposition 'from' (Direction & Spatial Relationship) ➔ 'My approach to teaching is quite different from my colleague's.'

quests.question: Are you ready ___ tomorrow's presentation?
quests.targetSentence: Are you ready for tomorrow's presentation?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Ready for' is followed by a noun, like a presentation; 'ready to' would instead need a verb, as in 'ready to present'.
quests.nativeTip: This word is followed by a noun naming what you're prepared for, not an action verb.
quests.visualAnchor: 🧭 Preposition 'for' (Direction & Spatial Relationship) ➔ 'Are you ready for tomorrow's presentation?'

quests.question: He's been worried ___ his upcoming medical results.
quests.targetSentence: He's been worried about his upcoming medical results.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Worried about' expresses anxiety toward a topic or event; 'worried for' would instead mean concern on behalf of another person.
quests.nativeTip: This is general anxiety about an upcoming event, not concern for someone else's safety.
quests.visualAnchor: 🧭 Preposition 'about' (Direction & Spatial Relationship) ➔ 'He's been worried about his upcoming medical results.'

quests.question: The whole project depends ___ getting approval from the board first.
quests.targetSentence: The whole project depends on getting approval from the board first.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Depend on' is correct here as well — the same fixed combination introduced earlier in this unit.
quests.nativeTip: One outcome relies on this condition being met, just like the earlier hiking example.
quests.visualAnchor: 🧭 Preposition 'on' (Surface Contact (e.g. on the table)) ➔ 'The whole project depends on getting approval from the board first.'

quests.question: I'm not very good ___ remembering names, so please forgive me if I forget yours.
quests.targetSentence: I'm not very good at remembering names, so please forgive me if I forget yours.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Good at' fits again here, describing a specific skill or ability, this time remembering names.
quests.nativeTip: This describes a skill, just like the puzzle-solving example earlier.
quests.visualAnchor: 🧭 Preposition 'at' (Specific Point (e.g. at the door)) ➔ 'I'm not very good at remembering names, so please forgive me if I forget yours.'

quests.spatialHierarchy: Enclosed Space / Volume (e.g. in the room)
quests.question: Despite the setbacks, she never stopped believing ___ her team's potential.
quests.targetSentence: Despite the setbacks, she never stopped believing in her team's potential.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Believe in' is the fixed combination for expressing trust or confidence in someone or something.
quests.nativeTip: Trust is placed inside an idea or a person's ability.
quests.visualAnchor: 🧭 Preposition 'in' (Enclosed Space / Volume (e.g. in the room)) ➔ 'Despite the setbacks, she never stopped believing in her team's potential.'

quests.question: He insisted ___ paying for everyone's dinner, even though we protested.
quests.targetSentence: He insisted on paying for everyone's dinner, even though we protested.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Insist on' is the fixed combination for firmly pushing for a particular action or outcome.
quests.nativeTip: This word connects insistence to the specific action being pushed for.
quests.visualAnchor: 🧭 Preposition 'on' (Surface Contact (e.g. on the table)) ➔ 'He insisted on paying for everyone's dinner, even though we protested.'

quests.question: Although she was initially afraid of failing the exam, she ended up being proud ___ her results.
quests.targetSentence: Although she was initially afraid of failing the exam, she ended up being proud of her results.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Proud of' returns here to close the unit, reinforcing the same pattern taught earlier in this level block.
quests.nativeTip: This links pride back to its cause, just like the earlier example about studying abroad.
quests.visualAnchor: 🧭 Preposition 'of' (Direction & Spatial Relationship) ➔ 'Although she was initially afraid of failing the exam, she ended up being proud of her results.'
